messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Darnell was 25, African American, and had built his life around being the one who noticed what others missed. As a journalist, he was used to moving through crowded streets, train platforms, and unfamiliar neighborhoods with a reporter’s alertness, and he had always taken pride in that ease. That changed one night after he was stopped by police on his way home from a late assignment. What began as a routine check quickly became frighteningly humiliating: a patrol car pulled in close, an officer ordered him out, and the tone shifted from clipped questions to hard suspicion. Darnell said the memory is still not organized like an ordinary recollection; it comes back with the force of being there again, more real and vivid than anything in daily life. He can still hear the footsteps coming up behind him on the pavement, the sound of boots closing the distance, and when he tries to explain the encounter he loses the thread and cannot finish, as if the scene breaks apart under his mouth. Since then, footsteps behind or nearby have become a potent jolt, and certain songs that were playing in his car earlier that evening can suddenly make his stomach drop, because they carry him back to the whole night in one instant. After those moments, he has come to scan the world as if danger is always a step away: he frequently looks behind him to check whether someone is following him, avoids unfamiliar places because he cannot assess the danger there, and finds it hard to concentrate long enough to read or draft copy without drifting back to the possibility of being cornered. He now wears concealing clothing, choosing darker, looser layers that make him feel less noticeable, and he has noticed that the more he hides, the more he convinces himself he is the kind of person who needs to hide. Darnell had also always associated journalism with curiosity and openness, but after the stop he began to tell himself that his life had been destroyed by the trauma, that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him, and that he used to be a happy person but now was always miserable. Those appraisals did not stay abstract; they made him pull back from the parts of life that once gave it texture. He started avoiding anything that reminded him of someone he had lost, including a close friend who had died the previous year, because grief already felt too close to the same rawness as the police encounter, and he made a point of avoiding anything that could cause negative or positive feelings alike, as though numbness were the only safe state left. Yet the more he shut down, the more convinced he became that he had already become less than himself, and that conviction deepened his misery.

The loop tightened in the weeks that followed. When he heard footsteps in the hallway outside his apartment or behind him on the sidewalk, the old scene would surge back with such vividness that he felt he had no choice but to change course, cross the street, keep his head down, or dress in a way that drew no attention. But those same protective habits kept feeding the fear. Concealing clothing made him feel hidden, yet also more on guard; avoiding unfamiliar places shrank his world and made every outing feel like a test he might fail; and cutting himself off from anything that stirred feeling left him flat and disconnected, which he then read as further proof that his life had been ruined. He noticed that once he had spent an hour checking behind him, or replaying the stop in his head, the memory became even more intrusive, almost as if the body had learned to summon it. Then the memory itself would sharpen the threat: he would hear the same footsteps in his mind, the same harsh cadence of the officers, and the remembered sounds would make the present street feel charged with danger. From there his thoughts would turn again to what the trauma meant about him—that he was not as capable as he had been, that the work that used to define him was slipping away, that he had become someone miserable and diminished—and with each return to that conclusion he became even more vigilant and more determined to avoid anything that might stir him up.

By the time he sought help, Darnell’s world had narrowed around these routines. His relationship had become strained by his withdrawal and emotional flatness, and at work he was increasingly unable to keep his attention on interviews in noisy public spaces or to move freely through the city the way his job required. What brought him in was the fear that his life was continuing to contract, that every month he was becoming more cautious, more isolated, and less like the journalist and partner he once believed himself to be. He wanted relief, but what frightened him most was the sense that one set of footsteps, one song, or one unexpected turn down an unfamiliar block could pull him straight back into that night and confirm that he was no longer the person he had been.
